forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?

(2) 14 Aug 2026, Consultancy.uk news/45353, Lesley Hornung of HLB International: AI is compressing delivery time, clients will 'ask harder questions about pricing and value', the billable-hour model faces a 'meaningful challenge', and automation reduces manual early-career work. forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is professional-services sectors losing a third or more of revenue or employment within roughly six years, with the loss primarily attributed to a single technology by multiple credible analyses. The class is thin. Travel agencies shed 40-50% of employment but over about fifteen years, and the automated function was transactional booking, not judgement. Legal document review contracted sharply but was a discrete commoditised task inside a larger sector rather than a sector. Typesetting, photo processing, stenography and directory assistance collapsed faster, but each was a craft occupation with one output a machine reproduced exactly. In every member of the class the automated thing was the whole product. Economic consultancy fails that test structurally: clients buy a bundle of quantitative analysis, testimony admissible before a court or regulator, relationship capital with counsel and agencies, political and legal cover, insurable accountability and a credential that survives cross-examination. AI compresses the analysis layer, perhaps a third to a half of delivered hours and less of the fee. The remaining layers plausibly appreciate as machine-generated analysis proliferates, because signing your name to a number before a tribunal is a liability transfer no model performs. Three adjustments push the base rate up. AI attacks the pyramid economics that fund senior capacity: Big Four graduate intake down 6-29%, McKinsey cutting ~10% of global headcount, BCG entry-level down 15%. Pricing is decoupling from hours, which can deflate sector revenue without demand loss. And the May 2026 Anthropic ($1.5bn, Blackstone and Hellman & Friedman) and OpenAI ($4bn+, TPG, Advent, Bain Capital, Brookfield) services joint ventures are the first credible AI-native entrants targeting the consulting pool. Scope matters: read narrowly as CRA, NERA, Cornerstone, Brattle, Compass Lexecon and Frontier, current evidence points the wrong way entirely. Outside view 5-12%, adjusted to 15-19% for the AI trajectory and entry-level compression, then discounted for the demanding 'primarily attributed to AI' bar. Central 16%.

TRIGGER CHECK. Trigger 1, the Clacton declaration (revise DOWN if Farage exceeds about 78 percent on turnout above 45 percent, revise UP if share is below about 62 percent or turnout under 30 percent): DID NOT FIRE on either strict limb, but PARTIALLY FIRED in the UP direction. Declared in the early hours of 14 August: Farage 22,239 votes, 63.3 percent, majority 12,784 over Count Binface on 9,455 and 26.9 percent; turnout 35,111 of 79,785, 44.4 percent, down 13.6 points on 2024 and the lowest since the seat was created. Coming in at 63.3 percent with a joke candidate on 26.9 percent is therefore an undershoot against expectations, and Bloomberg on 14 August reported Farage skipped the count and the victory events, saying he would not be demeaned by nobodies. The offsetting point: his raw vote of 22,239 exceeded his 21,225 in 2024. Trigger 4 (Met Section 61 arrest or charge, or Standards finding): DID NOT FIRE; still two interviewed under caution, early CPS advice, no arrests. Trigger 5 (Reform leads in three-plus houses in a fortnight, or Restore Britain below 2 percent): PARTIALLY FIRED. Find Out Now, fieldwork to 12 August, has Ref 24, Lab 22, Grn 14, a new Reform lead; with Freshwater on 10 August (Ref 26, Lab 23) and YouGov on 3 August (Ref 23, Lab 22) that is three houses inside a fortnight, though YouGov's 10 August reading flipped back to Lab 24, Ref 22. Restore Britain shows no collapse. Trigger 6 (Budget gilt selloff or Burnham net approval negative): DID NOT FIRE; analysts still expect yields to fall into the 28 October Budget. Judgement: the polling aggregate softened, but the outside-view anchor that was holding me down has moved. Ladbrokes now prices Labour most seats at 11/8 and Reform at 11/5, versus 13/8 and 7/4 in the prior, roughly 40 percent normalised against 35 percent. A market repricing toward my central plus an underwhelming Clacton share outweighs 0.7pp of aggregate drift, but only just, hence one point.
forecasts.base_rate: The reference class is a governing party roughly three years from a required election, having changed leader mid-term, running level or narrowly ahead in a fragmented five-party system. Three anchors. First, incumbency plus seat efficiency. Since 1945 the largest party at one election has usually been largest at the next, because first-past-the-post cushions vote loss for geographically efficient coalitions. Labour's 2024 vote, even shrunk to the mid-20s, remains the most efficiently distributed in Great Britain, which is why seat models keep putting Labour largest at vote shares at or below Reform's: PLMR/Electoral Calculus in July had Labour 217, Conservatives 151, Reform 127; PollCheck's demographic model has Labour largest; an April-May MRP had Labour 290-320. This vote-to-seat decoupling is the single most important structural fact here. Second, mid-term leadership changes. Major 1990 and Johnson 2019 went on to win most seats; Brown 2007 and Sunak 2022 did not, giving a base rate near 50 percent, with the caveat that the winners called early elections while the honeymoon lasted, an option Burnham retains. Third, poll-to-outcome mapping at T-36 months is weakly predictive, with large historic mean absolute errors and frequent lead reversals; Reform's own path from 31 percent in January to about 24 percent now illustrates the volatility. Right-of-centre fragmentation across Reform, the Conservatives and Restore Britain is the mechanism most likely to hand Labour a seat plurality on a historically low vote plurality. Two drags: governing parties in the mid-20s mid-term usually shed further support once a Budget imposes real costs, with 28 October the first hard test; and prediction markets, reasonably calibrated on UK seat questions, sit near 40 percent for Labour most seats, still below this central.

forecasts.base_rate: The structural base rate is set by publication mechanics, not historical frequency. Only five reference months, July through November 2026, publish before 1 January 2027, from the 19 August release to mid-December. December 2026 CPI publishes in mid-January 2027 and cannot count. So the question reduces to whether any one of five prints, starting from a 2.6% June base, comes in below 2.0%. UK CPI typically moves 0.1-0.3pp per month absent an administered price step. Falls of 0.7pp or more within four months from a 2.6% base occur in roughly 15-20% of historical windows, and almost all involve a falling energy cap or a VAT cut. Composition also blocks the path: services ran 3.6% in June at roughly 45-50% of the basket, so sub-2.0% headline would require goods near zero while energy rises, a configuration absent since 2015-16 and 2020. Theatrical cumulative grosses are monotonic in practice: refunds, comps and currency effects are absorbed inside reported figures rather than clawed back from prior totals. The largest genuinely contested restatements on record involve disputed territory reporting, most often China and India; even in the most-cited disputes the contested sums have been tens of millions on billion-dollar films, i.e. low single digits in percentage terms. forecasts.key_change: Hold at 99%, CI [98, 99]. No numerical move is available because the estimate is already at the operative ceiling, but the 13-15 August window delivered the single strongest confirmatory evidence since this question opened, and the probability mass inside the band has shifted decisively to the top. Two dated Bloomberg prints did the work. On 13 August Bloomberg reported that OpenAI's annualized revenue run rate has topped $40bn, roughly doubling from the above-$20bn exit CFO Sarah Friar cited for end-2025, with President Greg Brockman telling staff the monthly run rate grew more than 20% in July alone; the report was picked up by Reuters/Yahoo Finance, Investing.com, PYMNTS, Proactive Investors and TradingView on 13-14 August. This retires the stale '$25bn and flat since February' framing that was the single largest drag on this forecast, and it does so through a resolution-qualifying outlet. On 14 August Bloomberg reported Anthropic's Q2 2026 revenue exceeded $11.5bn against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m in Q2 2025, a 14-fold year-on-year increase, with positive adjusted operating income; The Information carried the same figure the same day. Bloomberg-only arithmetic therefore now stands at over $40bn plus a Q2 annualisation near $46bn, roughly $86bn combined, before any Q3 or Q4 growth. Surrounding items on 13-14 August: Qz, Fortune and Forbes reported Anthropic backers targeting a $2tn-plus October IPO with expectations of $100-120bn annualised revenue by end-2026; Fortune's sceptical 14 August piece, arguing the underlying business is nowhere near $2tn, nonetheless models a $10bn December month, which is a $120bn December run rate. OpenAI is still reported eyeing Q4, possibly September; 2027 remains an option, never a confirmation. 5 (qualifying print for both above $70bn combined): PARTIALLY FIRED. forecasts.base_rate: The governing reference class is 'threshold already crossed on the current published record, question asks whether it stays crossed and gets documented.' Such questions resolve YES at 95-99%; they require no new growth, only continuity plus publication. A second class is revenue-trajectory persistence for hypergrowth private software firms over a four-month horizon. Firms adding run-rate at these rates essentially never print an absolute quarterly decline absent a discrete shock such as product withdrawal, mass customer loss or fraud restatement. The one near-shock in this case, the June Commerce export controls that froze access to Mythos and Fable, was lifted by 30 June (CNN) and Q2 revenue still came in above $11.5bn. Anthropic's path ($9bn end-2025, $30bn April, $47bn disclosed May, Q2 recognised above $11.5bn) and OpenAI's (above $20bn end-2025, above $40bn per Bloomberg 13 August) both sit deep in the persistence regime. A third class is disclosure availability, which is the actually binding constraint. For high-salience private companies in live IPO processes, the probability that Bloomberg, The Information, FT or the company publishes a run-rate figure in any given quarter has been near-unity: Anthropic has had named-outlet prints in January, March, April, May and August 2026, OpenAI in February, May and now August. Two confidential S-1s under SEC review add a mandatory-disclosure channel. On accounting, forced gross-to-net restatements cut headline revenue 20-40% where they occur, in perhaps a fifth to a third of contested cases; current analyst modelling puts Anthropic's restatement path at 10%. Applying a punitive 40% haircut to a plausible Anthropic Q4 gross run-rate of $100-120bn still leaves $60-72bn, and OpenAI at $45-60bn takes the combined figure to $105-132bn. The threshold survives the worst plausible accounting outcome. Calibration anchor: where the quantity exceeds the bar by more than 20% and only a source technicality can defeat it, 98-99% is defensible; above 99 requires the Q4 print in hand.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD at 34%, CI [21,48] unchanged. Two genuinely new structural items arrived in the 13-15 August window and they roughly cancel. The upside item. ONS published business investment alongside the Q2 GDP first estimate on 13 August 2026: business investment rose 1.7% q/q in Q2, accelerating from 0.9% in Q1, and was 0.8% higher than a year earlier. That outturn directly contradicts the survey-based pessimism my prior leaned on, namely the BCC Q2 QES finding only 17% of firms planning to raise capex (a post-pandemic low, fieldwork 11 May to 8 June) and the BCC's forecast of business investment falling 2.2% in 2026. EY's UK Economic Outlook, published in the same window, nudged 2026 GDP to 0.9% from 0.8% in May and held 2027 at 1.2%, citing oil prices returning toward pre-conflict levels faster than expected. The downside item. Bloomberg Economics estimated on 14 August that this summer's prolonged heat has already cost the UK economy about GBP 6bn, roughly 0.2% of output, with 38.1C recorded on 13 August, wheat yields 14% below the ten-year average and June construction output at -0.1%. That is a dated, quantified read on exactly the recurring climate drag that would bite repeatedly across a 2030s decade average, and it is more relevant to a fourteen-year horizon than one quarter of capex. The OBR forecast commissioned by Healey on 21 July is still pending for 28 October; the IMF's 2026 Article IV (Board concluded 16 July) keeps potential at 1.4% and 2026 growth at 1.0%. Judgement: the core arithmetic is untouched. Roughly 1.0% trend productivity plus roughly 0.4% labour supply leaves potential near 1.4%, just under the bar, with a negatively skewed shock distribution and a fat but unproven AI tail. forecasts.base_rate: The naive outside view flatters the question. UK decade averages for annual real GDP growth were about 2.2% in the 1990s, 1.8% in the 2000s and 2.0% in the 2010s, with the 2020s running near 1.0% to date, so three of the last four decades cleared 1.5% and the unadjusted base rate is roughly 60-75%. That reference class is contaminated. Pre-2008 decades rested on labour productivity growth near 2% a year plus rapid labour force expansion from rising female participation and later EU accession migration; neither driver is available for the 2030s. The 2010s figure is itself misleading, resting on a deep post-crisis output gap that mechanically flattered measured growth through recovery rather than trend. The forward decomposition is the better anchor. Potential growth equals trend productivity plus trend labour input. The OBR's November 2025 forecast cut underlying medium-term productivity growth to 1.0% a year from 1.3%, and its March 2026 EFO retained 1.0%. The IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, assessed UK potential growth at 1.4% and judged the economy to have grown at potential in 2025. On labour supply, ONS 2024-based projections have natural change turning negative from 2026, with net migration falling sharply before stabilising, implying working-age population growth decelerating toward 0.3-0.5% a year across the 2030s and lower still if inactivity keeps drifting up from its current 9.11 million. Adding roughly 1.0-1.1% productivity to roughly 0.3-0.5% labour supply gives potential near 1.3-1.6%, straddling the threshold with the central estimate marginally below. Shocks are asymmetric against the question: a decade arithmetic mean is dragged down far more by one recession year than lifted by one boom year, and the 2030s carry non-trivial odds of at least one recession, energy shock, climate disruption or fiscal event. Medium-term official growth projections for OECD economies have also systematically overshot outturns since 2008.
